title: Warfarin, infection and bruising
brief: HMR referral: Mara, 76, lives independently and wants to keep managing her own medicines. She has atrial fibrillation, hypertension and osteoarthritis.
She bought aspirin for knee pain and started an antibiotic for a chest infection three days ago.
She reports new bruises and one episode of blood when brushing her teeth. Her last documented INR was 2.4 two weeks ago.
actor: If asked, Mara says she took aspirin most days this week because it worked better than paracetamol.
She has not told the INR clinic about the antibiotic. She is unsure of its name and has the box at home.
She has no black stools, severe headache, fall or persistent bleeding today, but the bruising is new.
key: Prioritise the possible bleeding/anticoagulation problem; assess current bleeding and urgent red flags, verify the antibiotic and arrange prompt INR/medical review as indicated.
Identify non-prescribed aspirin and assess safer pain options without making an unsupported warfarin dose change.
Check warfarin indication, target INR, adherence, monitoring process, interactions and who will contact the prescriber/INR clinic.
Give a clear contingency plan for significant bleeding or neurological symptoms and document communication.
questions: How do you rank the MRPs and why?
What information would change the urgency today?
What would you recommend about analgesia and monitoring?
What will you communicate to the GP and INR clinic?
How would you explain the plan to Mara without alarming her unnecessarily?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Diabetes, CKD and a recent illness
brief: HMR referral: Ravi, 69, has type 2 diabetes, CKD and hypertension. He lives with his partner and would prefer a simple regimen.
He has had vomiting and poor oral intake for 48 hours but continued his regular medicines. He reports two morning episodes of shakiness relieved by juice.
Recent eGFR was 38 mL/min/1.73 m²; HbA1c 7.1%.
actor: If asked, Ravi has not measured glucose during the shaky episodes.
He has passed less urine today and feels light-headed on standing.
He is worried that stopping any medicine, even briefly, will harm him.
key: Treat dehydration and possible hypoglycaemia as immediate safety concerns; assess severity and arrange timely medical assessment.
Review sick-day management for relevant diabetes and blood-pressure medicines using current course guidance, with a specific restart/monitoring plan agreed by the treating clinician.
Check renal function, current glucose, medicine doses, adherence and the patient's ability to monitor at home.
Avoid assuming the HbA1c alone shows safe control; integrate age, symptoms, CKD and preference for simplicity.
questions: Which problems need action today?
What further data would you obtain before changing long-term therapy?
How does CKD affect medicine safety?
How would you discuss a temporary sick-day plan?
Who will review the regimen after recovery?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Heart failure, blood pressure and ibuprofen
brief: HMR referral: Elaine, 73, has heart failure, hypertension and chronic back pain. She has new ankle swelling and has needed two pillows at night this week.
She sometimes skips her diuretic on days out because of toilet access. She bought ibuprofen for back pain this week.
Home BP readings average 156/88 mmHg; her weight is 2.5 kg above her usual value.
actor: If asked, she is more breathless walking to the letterbox but is comfortable at rest.
She bought ibuprofen because she did not realise it could affect her heart or kidneys.
She wants help finding a pain option that lets her stay active.
key: Recognise possible worsening heart failure and arrange prompt clinical assessment, escalating if severe breathlessness or chest pain emerges.
Identify ibuprofen and missed diuretic doses as contributors; review pain management and adherence barriers with the patient.
Request renal function, electrolytes, BP and weight trend before recommending regimen changes.
Agree a feasible monitoring and access plan with GP/cardiology and the patient.
questions: What are your top three MRPs?
What symptoms would require urgent care?
How would you address the diuretic adherence barrier?
What monitoring is needed?
How would you compare pain options in this patient?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Thyroid replacement and administration
brief: HMR referral: Zoe, 58, has hypothyroidism, iron-deficiency anaemia and reflux. She reports fatigue and has recently been told her TSH is above her laboratory's reference range.
She takes all tablets together with breakfast to avoid forgetting them.
The GP referral asks for review of her thyroid treatment.
actor: If asked, Zoe has used the same levothyroxine dose for years but started iron six weeks ago.
She sometimes misses weekend doses and is concerned about a complicated schedule.
She has no severe acute symptoms.
key: Investigate timing, adherence, recent changes and interacting products before recommending a dose change.
Ask for actual thyroid results, prior trend and the clinical indication/target; seek GP review and repeat testing after a consistent administration plan per current guidance.
Make the regimen workable for Zoe and explain why separation/consistency matters without prescribing a new dose independently.
Assess fatigue more broadly, including anaemia and other causes.
questions: What is the likely medication-related problem?
What additional history and results do you need?
What would you recommend today?
How would you make the schedule workable?
How would you monitor whether the change helped?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Depression, sleep and falls
brief: HMR referral: Nola, 79, reports low mood and poor sleep after a bereavement. She has fallen twice in three months and is afraid of losing independence.
She says her antidepressant has not helped, but the start date and adherence are unclear. Diazepam is used most nights.
Her daughter fills a weekly medicine organiser.
actor: If asked, Nola sometimes feels dizzy when rising and is sleepy in the morning.
She takes diazepam because she fears a sleepless night and does not want it stopped abruptly.
She denies immediate self-harm intent but says some days feel hopeless; a fuller risk assessment is needed.
key: Assess immediate mental-health safety and falls risk, including sedation, orthostasis and environmental factors.
Review cumulative sedative/anticholinergic burden and possible medicine-related falls; avoid abrupt benzodiazepine cessation.
Clarify antidepressant duration, adherence, response, function and preferences before considering a change with GP.
Propose a collaborative, staged plan with monitoring, supports and follow-up.
questions: Which issue is most urgent?
How would you assess depression response and safety?
Which medicines may contribute to falls?
How would you approach diazepam reduction?
Which other professionals or supports would you involve?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Asthma control and inhaler use
brief: HMR referral: James, 34, has asthma and allergic rhinitis. He has used a reliever on most days this month and wakes coughing twice a week.
His preventer refills have been irregular. He has no written asthma action plan.
He recently changed jobs and is exposed to dust.
actor: If asked, James avoids the preventer because he dislikes its taste and is unsure whether it is needed when he feels well.
He can speak comfortably now and has no current severe breathlessness.
He wants a plan that fits a rotating shift schedule.
key: Recognise poor control and assess current symptoms for urgent deterioration.
Check inhaler technique, actual use, device suitability, adherence barriers, triggers and rhinitis control before suggesting escalation.
Arrange prescriber review of controller regimen and a written action plan; counsel on monitoring and urgent warning signs.
Adapt the plan to shift work and patient preferences.
questions: What indicates poor control?
What would you assess before a medicine change?
How do you check device technique?
What is your follow-up plan?
What symptoms require immediate escalation?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Chronic pain with liver and renal risk
brief: HMR referral: Tomas, 67, has knee osteoarthritis, compensated chronic liver disease, CKD and a history of peptic ulcer disease. Pain is limiting his walks.
He takes paracetamol from two different products and naproxen bought at a supermarket. He drinks alcohol on some weekends and cannot recall the daily amounts of his pain medicines.
The GP requests a pain management review.
actor: If asked, Tomas often takes both paracetamol products on the same day without adding their doses.
He values walking to the shops and is open to non-medicine strategies.
No current gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms are reported, but these must be checked.
key: Reconcile all products and total daily exposure before making a dosing recommendation.
Identify NSAID-related renal, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular concerns and assess bleeding/alarm symptoms.
Set function-based goals and consider non-drug support plus patient-specific medicine options with the GP, verified against current AMH/eTG and labs.
Plan monitoring and a clear follow-up rather than offering a generic analgesic switch.
questions: Which risks make this case different from routine osteoarthritis?
What exactly must you ask about the OTC products?
How would you assess benefit?
Which non-drug options are realistic?
What would you communicate to the GP?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Discharge list and duplicate therapy
brief: HMR referral: Leila, 71, was discharged five days ago after an acute coronary syndrome. She has diabetes and hypertension and is confused by the new medicine list.
Her old weekly pack still contains medicines from before admission; she has been taking tablets from both the pack and new boxes.
She reports light-headedness.
actor: If asked, Leila has the discharge paperwork and all medicine boxes at home.
She has no current chest pain, shortness of breath or bleeding, but would need urgent assessment if these appear.
Her preferred pharmacy can repack the medicines once the list is confirmed.
key: Prioritise urgent reconciliation and assess symptoms/vitals; do not assume the old pack or discharge list alone is correct.
Identify potential duplication and omission, especially antiplatelet and statin regimen, and verify with discharge team/GP/pharmacy.
Create one confirmed current list, organise pack changes and teach Leila how to use it.
Monitor BP, pulse, bleeding and adverse effects with clear responsibilities and contingency advice.
questions: How do you verify the intended regimen?
Which discrepancies matter most today?
What would you do with the existing pack?
How do you counsel on antiplatelet safety?
How will you confirm the problem is resolved?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: A child's spreading skin lesions
brief: You are the pharmacist. A parent asks for something for their 6-year-old child's yellow-crusted sores around the nose. The child is at school and is not present.
Manage the presentation, including whether it can be handled in your setting and what the parent should do next.
actor: Child weighs about 21 kg; parent can confirm exact weight. Lesions began four days ago and have spread from one to several spots.
No fever, lethargy or rapidly spreading redness. No known medicine allergies; no regular medicines or chronic conditions.
A sibling has a similar lesion. Parent is worried about school attendance and wants antibiotics immediately.
key: Confirm who the patient is, age/weight, history, medicines, conditions and allergy/adverse effects.
Assess distribution, severity, systemic signs, alternatives and eligibility/referral criteria in the current Queensland Health impetigo guideline.
Discuss appropriate hygiene, spread prevention, treatment or referral according to scope, and school/daycare advice from current local guidance.
Give a clear beneficial outcome, review point and safety net if fever, worsening redness or poor response.
questions: What would make this presentation outside scope?
How would you discuss antibiotic stewardship with the parent?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: impetigo (supplied PDF p. 97)

title: Shingles near the eye
brief: A 62-year-old asks for a cream for a painful blistering rash on one side of the forehead. They say it started yesterday.
Manage the request in a 10-minute pharmacy consultation.
actor: If asked, the rash extends to the eyelid and the eye feels gritty; vision seems slightly blurred.
The patient takes no regular medicines and reports no allergies. They had chickenpox as a child.
They hope to avoid a doctor because of work commitments.
key: Identify possible ocular involvement and arrange urgent medical/eye assessment rather than routine pharmacy treatment.
Clarify onset, rash distribution, eye/neurological symptoms, immune status, pregnancy, medicines and allergies.
Explain the urgency in patient-centred terms and help them access care now.
Counsel on avoiding contact with vulnerable people and give a contingency plan using current guidance.
questions: Which features change the referral urgency?
How would you respond if the patient declines referral?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: herpes zoster (supplied PDF p. 71)

title: Painful swimmer's ear
brief: A 28-year-old swimmer asks for ear drops because the right ear hurts after several days at the pool.
Assess and manage the request.
actor: Pain is worse when the outer ear is moved; there is mild itch and scant discharge.
No fever, severe pain, dizziness or facial weakness. No diabetes or immunosuppression. No known allergies; no regular medicines.
They used a cotton bud yesterday and are unsure whether the eardrum is intact.
key: Confirm patient and full critical history; assess red flags, tympanic membrane concerns and differential diagnosis.
Use the current otitis externa guideline to determine examination, eligibility and treatment/referral requirements.
Explain ear care, correct use of any chosen treatment, water avoidance and when to return.
Avoid selecting a potentially unsuitable drop without checking eardrum status and guideline restrictions.
questions: What would make you refer rather than treat?
How does possible perforation alter the choice?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: acute otitis externa (supplied PDF p. 33)

title: Hay fever that is not controlled
brief: A 23-year-old wants a stronger product for daily sneezing and a blocked nose. A non-sedating antihistamine has helped only a little.
Provide a patient-centred pharmacy consultation.
actor: Symptoms occur most days in spring, with itchy eyes. No fever, unilateral bleeding or facial pain.
They tried a nasal corticosteroid for two days, then stopped because it seemed ineffective. They are not pregnant, take no other medicines and have no known allergies.
They need to stay alert while driving for work.
key: Confirm symptoms and consider allergic versus nonallergic rhinitis and red flags.
Check how prior medicines were used, technique and adequate trial before recommending a change.
Discuss suitable options, onset/expectations, technique, non-drug measures and driving preference using current guideline.
Set a review point and escalation criteria.
questions: What changes your diagnosis?
How would you check nasal spray technique?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: rhinitis (supplied PDF p. 54)

title: Reflux with an alarm feature
brief: A 54-year-old asks for omeprazole for worsening heartburn. They have taken antacids for months.
Assess the presentation and decide what happens today.
actor: On questioning, food has recently felt stuck when swallowing and they have lost weight without trying.
They use ibuprofen several days a week for back pain. No known allergies; no other medicines reported.
They want a quick product because they are travelling soon.
key: Elicit dysphagia and weight loss and arrange timely medical assessment; do not simply supply symptom suppression.
Review duration, severity, bleeding symptoms, medicines, red flags and alternative diagnoses.
Explain the reason for referral clearly and assist with access; discuss interim measures within safe scope.
Document advice and give escalation instructions for severe or worsening symptoms.
questions: Which symptoms are alarm features?
How does ibuprofen affect the assessment?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: GORD (supplied PDF p. 63)

title: Vomiting and reduced urine
brief: A parent asks for a medicine to stop their 2-year-old's vomiting after a day of gastroenteritis symptoms.
Manage the request.
actor: The child weighs 12 kg, has vomited repeatedly and has had few wet nappies today. The parent says the child is less active than usual.
There is no blood in vomit or stool. The child has no known allergies, regular medicines or major conditions.
The parent has tried small sips of juice but they have not stayed down.
key: Confirm age/weight, hydration status, frequency/duration, red flags, medicines, conditions and allergy/adverse effects.
Recognise reduced urine and reduced activity as concerning; arrange prompt medical assessment rather than an automatic antiemetic supply.
Explain appropriate oral rehydration advice only if safe while care is accessed, and what signs warrant urgent escalation.
Address the parent's immediate practical concern and help arrange a beneficial outcome.
questions: How do you assess dehydration?
What would change the urgency?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: acute nausea/vomiting (supplied PDF p. 22)

title: Knee pain and an NSAID request
brief: A 72-year-old asks for a strong anti-inflammatory tablet for a painful knee after gardening yesterday.
Assess and manage the request.
actor: No major injury, fever, inability to bear weight or hot swollen joint. They have CKD and take an ARB and a diuretic.
They used ibuprofen yesterday and had dizziness on standing today. No known medicine allergies.
Their goal is to walk comfortably to the shops next week.
key: Confirm patient, injury mechanism, pain features, function, red flags and complete medicine/condition/allergy history.
Identify renal/dehydration concerns with oral NSAIDs in this patient; assess dizziness and whether medical review is needed.
Discuss patient-specific non-drug and medicine options only after checking current AMH/guideline, and support the functional goal.
Safety-net for worsening pain, swelling, systemic symptoms or reduced urine.
questions: Which medicines and conditions change analgesic choice?
What would make this an urgent referral?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: mild acute musculoskeletal pain (supplied PDF p. 123)

title: Contraception continuation request
brief: A 29-year-old asks for a continuation of their combined oral contraceptive prescription because their GP appointment is in three weeks.
Conduct the consultation and decide on a safe plan.
actor: They have taken the same pill for two years. They report episodes of visual zig-zags followed by headache in the past six months, but have not mentioned them to a clinician.
No current pregnancy symptoms; one pill was missed last week. They do not smoke and take no other medicines. No known allergies.
They are anxious about a gap in contraception.
key: Assess pregnancy risk, missed pills, relevant medical history, BP, migraine symptoms, contraindications and current guideline eligibility.
Recognise possible migraine with aura as a safety concern for combined hormonal contraception and refer for appropriate review rather than routine continuation.
Address immediate contraception needs with guideline-consistent interim advice, including emergency contraception assessment if indicated.
Use shared decision making and clear follow-up.
questions: Which history changes eligibility?
How do you avoid leaving the patient without a contraception plan?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: hormonal contraception (supplied PDF p. 81)

title: New antibiotic with warfarin
brief: You are the pharmacist. Evelyn, 74, presents a prescription from Dr M. Patel for clarithromycin 500 mg tablets: take one tablet every 12 hours for 7 days; quantity 14, no repeats. The prescription states “chest infection”.
The dispensing record shows warfarin with a variable dose managed by an INR clinic. Evelyn asks to collect the antibiotic quickly and leave.
Assess the prescription and the person, then explain and carry out a safe plan.
actor: If asked, Evelyn takes variable warfarin doses and has not had an INR for about three weeks. She has not yet told the INR clinic about this prescription.
She has a cough but no fever, severe breathlessness or chest pain. She noticed mild blood in her urine today; ask further about bleeding and escalation.
She has no known medicine allergies and also takes perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly.
key: Confirm patient, indication, symptoms, medicine history, medical conditions and allergies; assess haematuria and other urgent features.
Check clarithromycin with warfarin and other current medicines in AMH/eTG, and contact the prescriber and INR service for a coordinated antibiotic and monitoring plan before supply.
Explain the safety concern and next steps respectfully; do not independently alter warfarin dosing without a supported plan.
Provide clear bleeding and infection safety-net advice and document the outcome.
questions: What information do you need from the prescription?
Who do you contact and what do you say?
sources: Australian Government, Guiding Principles for Medication Management in the Community

title: Eczema flare or infection?
brief: An adult with known atopic dermatitis asks for a stronger steroid because a patch on the forearm has become very red and weepy.
Assess and manage the request.
actor: The patch is more painful than usual and has honey-coloured crusting. There is no fever or rapidly spreading redness.
They use an emollient inconsistently and a mild topical corticosteroid. No other medicines or known allergies.
They have a family event and want it improved quickly.
key: Clarify whether this is a simple flare, secondary infection or another diagnosis and assess extent/systemic symptoms.
Check medicine use, application technique, previous response and guideline eligibility.
Avoid simply escalating steroid potency without addressing possible infection and referral/treatment requirements.
Explain skin care, treatment plan, infection precautions, follow-up and safety net.
questions: What clues suggest secondary infection?
How would you counsel on emollients and topical therapy?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: atopic dermatitis (supplied PDF p. 140)

title: Psoriasis flare on sensitive sites
brief: A 46-year-old with known plaque psoriasis requests a repeat of the strong steroid they previously used on elbows. They now have a rash on the face and groin.
Conduct the consultation.
actor: The facial/groin rash is new and has not been diagnosed. They also describe new painful swollen fingers in the morning.
No fever. They use a topical steroid intermittently and take no other regular medicines. No known allergies.
They are embarrassed by the rash and want a discreet plan.
key: Establish site, diagnosis certainty, extent, previous treatments and symptoms of psoriatic arthritis.
Recognise sensitive-site and joint concerns that need medical assessment; avoid routine use of a potent steroid there.
Respect privacy, explain referral and interim skin care within scope.
Plan follow-up and urgent escalation for severe or rapidly worsening symptoms.
questions: Which features change scope?
How do you address privacy and patient preference?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: mild plaque psoriasis (supplied PDF p. 1)

title: Smoking cessation with a treatment preference
brief: A 41-year-old asks for help quitting smoking before a planned surgery in eight weeks. They want to know whether nicotine replacement might help.
Run a 10-minute patient-centred consultation.
actor: They smoke about 15 cigarettes a day and usually light the first within 30 minutes of waking. They tried quitting once and relapsed during a stressful week.
They take sertraline, have no known allergies, are not pregnant and prefer a plan they can afford.
Their partner smokes at home but is willing to support a quit attempt.
key: Assess readiness, dependence, prior attempts, triggers, medical/medicine history and treatment preferences.
Use current guideline to discuss behavioural support and suitable pharmacotherapy; verify product, dose and precautions in AMH before recommending.
Set a quit date or next step, practical support and a follow-up plan.
Discuss smoke exposure and relapse as part of learning, not failure.
questions: What would shape product choice?
How would you support a relapse?
sources: Queensland Health acute condition guideline: smoking cessation (supplied PDF p. 166)

title: Lost opioid dose, distressed patient
brief: A patient on a supervised opioid treatment program says they lost today's dose and demands a replacement immediately. They are visibly distressed and raising their voice.
Respond as the pharmacist. Focus on communication and professional responsibilities.
actor: The patient is worried about withdrawal and missing work. They calm somewhat if you acknowledge this and speak privately.
They say the dose was lost on the bus. They do not have a replacement authority or confirmed direction from the prescriber.
They resist being told to 'just call tomorrow' but will accept a concrete plan for today.
key: Listen and acknowledge the patient's distress and immediate goal; move to a private, safe space if possible.
Avoid promising or supplying a replacement outside the applicable program and legal requirements; verify records and contact the authorised prescriber/service.
Explain what can be done now, discuss urgent clinical support if withdrawal or safety concerns arise, and agree on next steps.
Maintain calm, respectful boundaries and document the interaction.
questions: How would you state the boundary without sounding accusatory?
What is the practical plan if the prescriber cannot be reached?
sources: Queensland Health QScript and medicines guidance

title: Parent angry about no antibiotic
brief: A parent says, 'The last pharmacist gave my child antibiotics. Why won't you? You're wasting my time.' The child has a cold-like illness and the parent is frustrated.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: The parent is worried because the child missed school and they have missed work.
They will describe symptoms if asked calmly. They have not been given a clear reason why antibiotics may be unsuitable.
They are willing to consider a safety-net plan if they feel heard.
key: Find the parent's goal and concern before giving an explanation.
Use plain language and avoid criticising the prior clinician; assess red flags and offer appropriate evaluation or referral.
Explain antibiotic stewardship and symptomatic options in a way responsive to the child's presentation.
Agree on what to watch for, when to seek care and how to access it.
questions: How would you repair rapport after the opening statement?
What if the child appears unwell?

title: Family member asks for private results
brief: A patient's adult daughter asks you to tell her what new medicine her father collected and why. She says she always helps him and becomes offended when you hesitate.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: The daughter is genuinely worried and says he has become forgetful.
No consent or legal authority to share his record is documented. The patient is not present.
She is open to asking him to join a conversation if the offer is respectful.
key: Acknowledge concern and explain confidentiality in plain language without disclosing patient-specific information.
Explore whether consent/authority can be established and offer to speak together with the patient or arrange a supported review.
Address immediate safety concerns through an appropriate route without unnecessary disclosure.
Remain warm and firm; avoid implying the daughter has done something wrong.
questions: What can you say without revealing private details?
What if she reports an immediate safety risk?

title: Dispensing error disclosed
brief: A patient returns after noticing that the medicine in their bag has a different strength from the label. They are frightened and ask whether they have been harmed.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: They took one dose last night but have no current symptoms. They are worried the pharmacy will hide the mistake.
The product and prescription need verification before giving a risk assessment.
They want a clear explanation and to know what happens next.
key: Respond promptly, apologise appropriately and assess immediate clinical risk; do not speculate before checking facts.
Verify prescription, product, dose taken and patient factors; arrange urgent clinical advice if indicated.
Explain the corrected supply and follow-up, documentation, incident process and who will contact them.
Be honest, calm and accountable without shifting blame.
questions: What do you do first?
How do you communicate uncertainty honestly?

title: Prescriber challenges your concern
brief: You phone a prescriber about a potential medicine interaction. They say, 'I've prescribed this for years. Just dispense it.' You still have a patient-safety concern.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: The prescriber is pressed for time and has not heard the specific patient factors.
They become more receptive if you state the concrete risk, relevant evidence and a workable option succinctly.
They can agree to a monitoring plan or alternative if discussed clearly.
key: Stay respectful and assert the patient-specific concern clearly, using structured communication.
State what is known, what needs checking and a practical recommendation or monitoring option.
Confirm the agreed plan, responsibility, timing and documentation before supply.
Escalate through appropriate clinical channels if a serious safety issue remains unresolved.
questions: How would you phrase the concern in 30 seconds?
What if they still refuse to engage?

title: Cost blocks the agreed plan
brief: A patient says the medicine you recommended is unaffordable and that previous pharmacists have made them feel judged. They are about to leave without treatment.
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: They can pay for a less expensive option but do not want to disclose personal finances at the counter.
They are open to discussing alternatives in private and appreciate a written simple plan.
Their main goal is symptom relief while staying within budget.
key: Acknowledge the concern without judgement and offer privacy.
Clarify the patient's goal and constraints, then explore clinically appropriate alternatives, subsidies or referral where relevant.
Check understanding and agree on an affordable, safe next step.
Avoid promising equivalence before checking the medicine and indication.
questions: How do you invite a cost discussion respectfully?
What if no affordable safe option is available today?

title: Patient refuses urgent referral
brief: You have advised urgent medical review for a concerning symptom. The patient says, 'I'm not going to hospital. I had a terrible experience there.'
Respond as the pharmacist.
actor: They fear being dismissed and leaving their child without care. They will explain these barriers if asked.
They can understand information and make their own decision. Their symptoms still need urgent assessment.
They may accept an alternative urgent care pathway or support person if options are discussed.
key: Listen to the previous experience and barriers, then explain the specific concern and urgency in plain language.
Respect autonomy while checking understanding and capacity; offer practical ways to access appropriate urgent care.
Give clear safety-net advice if they decline and document the discussion.
Do not use threats, blame or false reassurance.
questions: What do you say if they continue to decline?
How would you address the childcare barrier?

title: Colleague bypasses an allergy alert
brief: A busy colleague says an allergy alert is probably wrong and asks you to hand over the prescription without checking. The patient is waiting and the queue is growing.
Respond to the colleague and protect the patient.
actor: The colleague is stressed, not hostile, and thinks the recorded reaction was only nausea.
The actual reaction and medicine have not yet been verified with the patient or record.
They will agree to a brief safety check if you propose a quick clear process.
key: Speak up calmly and stop an unsafe handover until the alert is clarified.
Verify the patient, medicine and reaction history; distinguish allergy from adverse effect and involve the prescriber if needed.
Explain the brief delay to the patient without blaming a colleague.
Confirm and document the final plan while maintaining teamwork.
questions: How do you phrase the challenge to your colleague?
What if the reaction turns out to be severe?
